name: VFX / compositing treatment
controls: Optical, photographic, digital and simulated effects applied on top of the designed graphics: blur, light, shadow and reflection passes, lens and signal artifacts, temporal effects, particles and simulations.
question: Which effects, if any, should sit on top of the graphics?
notes: Effects are applied treatments, not the design itself; the strongest product motion usually uses one or none. Several terms overlap with other dimensions: grain, noise, scanlines and VHS are also texture options (there, a persistent surface; here, an effect you can dial or trigger); shadows are also their own dimension (there, the shadow style of the design; here, the compositing pass); glitch appears as texture, effect and transition. Pick the dimension that matches the intent: persistent look, applied treatment, or cut between scenes. Commonly confused pairs: bloom is light bleeding from the brightest parts of the whole image (threshold-based, camera-like) while glow is a halo attached to chosen elements regardless of brightness; chromatic aberration is an optical lens error with color fringes that grow toward the frame edges, while RGB split is a deliberate uniform offset of color channels; displacement moves pixels according to a map, distortion is any geometric warp (displacement is one way to do it); trails are decaying after-images, echo is discrete repeated copies, smear is the object itself stretched along its path for a frame or two. Browser feasibility matters in a HyperFrames build: CSS filter (blur, drop-shadow, brightness, hue-rotate) and backdrop-filter are cheap; SVG filters (feGaussianBlur, feDisplacementMap, feTurbulence, feColorMatrix, feMorphology, feSpecularLighting) cover most compositing effects but are expensive full-frame; canvas 2D handles particles and pixel work; WebGL (Three.js, shaders) is required for true refraction, volumetric smoke, fluid, cloth and soft-body simulation, or those should be pre-rendered footage. Every effect must be driven by the paused GSAP timeline (seek-safe): no CSS animation, no requestAnimationFrame clocks, no unseeded randomness; seed particle systems and step them deterministically from timeline time. Restraint rule: an effect should support one story beat; if it runs through the entire piece it is really a texture or a style.

options.what: No compositing effects: the designed graphics are rendered exactly as drawn.
options.looks: Crisp, unfiltered shapes, type and UI; nothing optical or simulated.
options.motion: Choreography, easing and layout changes carry all of the energy.
options.use: SaaS product films, UI demos, data visualization, Swiss and minimalist motion, anything that must read as precise.
options.vs: Clean texture concerns surface grain; no effects concerns applied treatments. A piece can be clean here and still carry film grain as texture.
options.prompt: Use no compositing effects: no blur, glow, bloom, grain, aberration, particles or distortion. Motion, layout and color carry the piece. The only permitted optical treatment is a design-level shadow if the shadow dimension calls for one.

options.what: Blur along an object's direction of travel, proportional to its speed, as a camera shutter records fast motion.
options.looks: Fast-moving elements streak softly along their path; static elements stay sharp; motion feels filmed rather than computed.
options.motion: Appears only during fast moves, peaking at maximum velocity and vanishing as the object settles.
options.use: Fast kinetic type, snappy transitions, whip moves, any piece that should feel cinematic rather than digital.
options.conveys: Speed, weight, filmic realism; removes the strobing of crisp fast motion.
options.vs: Directional blur is a static stylistic blur in one direction regardless of motion; motion blur is tied to actual velocity. Smear is a drawn deformation, not a blur.
options.prompt: Add velocity-linked motion blur to fast moves only: apply an SVG feGaussianBlur with stdDeviation set on the axis of travel only (e.g. '12 0' for horizontal moves) and tween it from 0 to peak and back to 0 in sync with the move's velocity curve (peak at mid-move for power3.inOut). Peak blur about 1-1.5% of the travel distance per frame. Do not blur type during holds or moves slower than 300px per second. The browser has no native shutter blur; this approximation is enough for video.

options.what: A uniform blur along one axis applied as a stylistic look, independent of actual motion.
options.looks: Elements smeared horizontally or vertically into soft streaks, often with a sharp copy on top; speed-lines feel even in a still frame.
options.motion: Used as a transition state (element streaks in, resolves sharp) or as a persistent speed motif.
options.use: Sports, automotive and energetic brand motion, transitions, fashion and music graphics.
options.vs: Motion blur follows velocity; directional blur is applied at a chosen amount regardless of speed. Light streaks are luminous; directional blur is a blur of the object itself.
options.prompt: Use directional blur as a transition state: elements enter with feGaussianBlur stdDeviation '30 0' (horizontal) and scaleX 1.3, resolving to '0 0' and scaleX 1 over 300-400ms with expo.out. Optionally keep a faint blurred copy at 20% behind the sharp element for 200ms after arrival. Limit to one axis per piece.

options.what: Blur of everything outside the focal plane, as from a lens with a wide aperture.
options.looks: One plane sharp, nearer and farther planes progressively blurred; bright points in blurred areas become soft discs (bokeh).
options.motion: Focus stays on the subject as it moves, or shifts between planes (rack focus, see camera).
options.use: 2.5D and 3D scenes, spatial UI, product hero shots, cinematic brand films.
options.conveys: Cinematic quality, focus, intimacy, premium feel.
options.vs: Depth of field is the static blur state; rack focus (camera) is the move that changes it. Directional and motion blur are about movement, not distance.
options.prompt: Apply depth of field by layer distance: filter: blur(0) on the focal layer, 3-5px for one layer away, 8-14px for two layers away; add 3-6 soft bokeh discs (radial-gradient circles, 20-40% opacity) in the farthest layer. Never put text on a blurred layer. In Three.js use a bokeh post-processing pass with focus tied to the hero object.

options.what: Optical bending of straight lines toward (barrel) or away from (pincushion) the frame center, as a real lens produces.
options.looks: Slightly bulging frame, lines curving near edges, sometimes with vignetting and edge softness; photographic authenticity.
options.motion: Distortion can intensify during fast camera moves or punch-ins, then relax.
options.use: Cinematic and filmed-looking graphics, compositing graphics into footage, energetic punch-in transitions.
options.vs: Fisheye is an extreme ultra-wide barrel distortion used as a style; lens distortion is usually subtle and realistic. Distortion (general) is any warp, not necessarily optical.
options.prompt: Apply subtle barrel distortion to the whole frame (3-6% bulge at edges) with a matching vignette (edges 15-20% darker). In the browser use an SVG feDisplacementMap driven by a radial displacement map image, or a WebGL post pass. For punch-ins, tween the distortion from 3% to 12% and back over 300ms alongside a 1.05 scale.

options.what: Extreme barrel distortion of an ultra-wide lens, bending the frame into a sphere around its center.
options.looks: Center enlarged and bulging, edges compressed and curved, often a circular or heavily vignetted frame; 90s skate video and hip-hop heritage.
options.motion: Elements rushing toward the lens swell dramatically; camera moves feel exaggerated and physical.
options.use: Streetwear, skate and music culture, playful social content, comedic emphasis.
options.vs: Lens distortion is subtle and realistic; fisheye is extreme and stylized.
options.prompt: Apply a strong spherical fisheye to the scene: center magnified about 1.4x, edges compressed, with a circular vignette. Use a WebGL post pass or an SVG feDisplacementMap with a pre-made spherical displacement map (scale 80-140). Elements approaching the center should scale faster than linearly. Keep type that must be read near the center.

options.what: Light bleeding outward from the brightest parts of the image, as overexposed highlights spill in a camera or eye.
options.looks: Bright areas (highlights, white type, lights) surrounded by a soft luminous haze; overall image feels luminous and slightly dreamy.
options.motion: Intensity follows brightness: as an element brightens, its bloom grows; flashes and light sweeps bloom briefly.
options.use: Cinematic brand films, 3D product renders, neon and night scenes, dramatic reveals.
options.vs: Glow is a halo attached to chosen elements regardless of brightness; bloom applies to whatever is brightest in the image, via a threshold.
options.prompt: Add bloom as a threshold pass: duplicate the frame, keep only the brightest pixels (feColorMatrix or feComponentTransfer threshold at about 85% luminance), blur them (stdDeviation 12-24), and composite back with mix-blend-mode: screen at 40-60%. In Three.js use UnrealBloomPass (threshold 0.8-0.9, strength 0.6-1.0). Keep bloom off UI text at rest; let it swell only on reveals and light flashes.

options.what: A soft colored halo applied around specific elements, as if they emit light.
options.looks: Chosen lines, icons, type or UI edges surrounded by a soft colored aura; the element reads as a light source.
options.motion: Glow pulses, ignites on activation, travels along strokes, dims when inactive.
options.use: Neon and cyberpunk styles, AI and futuristic UI, active states and highlights, dark UI accents.
options.vs: Bloom is threshold-based and applies to all bright areas; glow is attached to chosen elements. Glow instead of shadow (shadow dimension) uses glow for elevation on dark UI.
options.prompt: Apply glow only to the active or hero element: stacked drop-shadow filters in the element's color (0 0 4px at 90%, 0 0 12px at 60%, 0 0 32px at 30%). Ignite glows over 200-300ms (power2.out) when an element activates and dim them to 30% when inactive. Never glow body text; never glow more than two elements at once.

options.what: Bright streaks or bands of light crossing the frame: anamorphic lens flares, light leaks or specular sweeps.
options.looks: Long thin horizontal flares, warm orange-red film light leaks from frame edges, or a bright diagonal band sweeping across a surface.
options.motion: Streaks sweep across in 300-900ms on reveals and transitions; leaks bloom in and fade; flares follow a light source.
options.use: Logo reveals, product hero shots, cinematic titles, tech launch films, transitions.
options.vs: Glow stays attached to an element; light streaks travel through the frame. Bloom is a halo around brightness, not a moving band. Light wipe (transitions) uses a streak as a cut.
options.prompt: Add one light streak per reveal: a thin horizontal band (2-6px core, 120-200px soft falloff, white core with an accent-tinted edge) with mix-blend-mode: screen, sweeping across the hero element in 500-800ms (power2.inOut), clipped to the element for a specular sweep or full-frame for an anamorphic flare. No more than one streak per 5 seconds.

options.what: Composited shadows that ground objects and show their height above a surface.
options.looks: Soft offset shadows beneath cards, objects and type; shadow size and softness indicate elevation.
options.motion: Shadows grow, soften and fade as objects lift; shrink and sharpen as they land; shift with the implied light direction.
options.use: UI and card animation, product shots, paper and layered 2D styles, any piece with implied depth.
options.vs: The shadow dimension defines the shadow style (soft, hard, long); this effect option means adding a physically behaving shadow pass. Ambient shadows are contact darkening, not cast shadows.
options.prompt: Composite one consistent light source (top-left, about 30 degrees) and give every elevated element a shadow whose offset, blur and opacity track its height: at rest 0 2px 4px at 12%, lifted 0 16px 32px at 18%, with shadow tweens on the same timeline as the lift. Shadows never change direction within a scene.

options.what: Soft darkening where surfaces meet or come close, independent of a directional light.
options.looks: Subtle dark gradients in corners, under objects resting on a surface and between close elements; grounds objects without an obvious light.
options.motion: Contact darkening tightens as an object touches down and diffuses as it lifts away.
options.use: 3D product renders, soft 3D and clay styles, premium UI shots, isometric scenes.
options.vs: Cast shadows project away from a light; ambient shadows sit directly where surfaces meet. Inner shadow (shadow dimension) is an inset style on flat UI.
options.prompt: Add ambient contact shadows: a tight, dark ellipse directly under each resting object (radial-gradient, 25-35% black at center, width 80-90% of the object, height 8-12% of width), plus soft darkening in inner corners. As an object lifts, widen and fade the ellipse (opacity to 8%, scale 1.3) on the same tween. In Three.js use contact shadows or an SSAO pass.

options.what: Solid, unblurred shadows offset diagonally behind an element, a graphic rather than physical device.
options.looks: A crisp copy of the element's shape in black or a strong color offset 4-12px down and right; neo-brutalist and retro print look.
options.motion: On press, the element slides into its shadow (offset collapses to 0) and pops back; shadows can extend on hover.
options.use: Neo-brutalist UI, playful SaaS, retro and print-inspired brand motion, sticker styles.
options.conveys: Boldness, playfulness, graphic confidence, raw honesty.
options.vs: Soft shadows imply real light; hard offset shadows are a graphic device. Extruded 2D (depth) fills the gap between face and offset; a hard shadow leaves a gap.
options.prompt: Give cards, buttons and key shapes a hard offset shadow: box-shadow 6px 6px 0 #111 (no blur), paired with a 2px solid #111 border. On press, translate the element 6px, 6px while shadow offset tweens to 0 in 80-120ms (power2.out), then release back. All shadows share one offset direction and size.

options.what: Mirror images of objects on glossy floors or surfaces, and environment reflections on glossy objects.
options.looks: A faded, flipped copy of an object below it on a glossy floor; or window and light reflections sliding across screens and surfaces.
options.motion: Reflections move in lockstep with objects; surface reflections slide as objects turn.
options.use: Product hero shots, device reveals, premium tech launch films, Web 2.0 styles.
options.vs: Refraction bends light through a transparent object; reflection bounces it off a surface. Chrome (material) is a reflective material; reflections here are a compositing pass.
options.prompt: Add a floor reflection under hero objects: a vertically flipped copy (scaleY -1) directly below, masked with a linear-gradient from 25% opacity at the contact line to 0 over 30-40% of the object height, blurred 1-2px. For screens, add a faint diagonal glare band (white 6-10%) that slides as the device rotates. Reflections move on the same tweens as the objects.

options.what: The bending of what lies behind a transparent object (glass, water, crystal) as light passes through it.
options.looks: Background content warped, magnified or offset within the shape of a glass or liquid element; edges show the strongest bending.
options.motion: Distortion shifts as the transparent object moves over content, which is what makes the effect read.
options.use: Glass and liquid-glass UI, premium abstract 3D, water and beverage films, AI brand motion.
options.vs: Reflection mirrors light off a surface; refraction bends it through a volume. Displacement (signal) is the technique usually used to fake refraction in 2D.
options.prompt: Fake refraction by displacing a copy of the background inside the transparent shape: clip a duplicate of the underlying layer to the shape and apply an SVG feDisplacementMap (scale 15-40) driven by a map that is strongest at the edges (radial or edge gradient). Move the shape over detailed content (type, UI, stripes) so the bending reads. Physically correct refraction requires WebGL (Three.js MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission).

options.what: An optical lens error in which color channels focus at slightly different places, producing color fringes that increase toward the frame edges.
options.looks: Thin red/cyan or purple/green fringes on high-contrast edges, strongest in the corners, absent in the center; photographic imperfection.
options.motion: Intensity can spike during fast moves and punch-ins, then relax; fringes scale radially with distance from center.
options.use: Cinematic and filmed-looking graphics, compositing into footage, subtle energy accents on camera moves.
options.conveys: Lens realism, physicality, cinematic texture; heavy use reads as edgy.
options.vs: RGB split is a uniform digital offset in a chosen direction, often large and glitchy; chromatic aberration is radial, subtle and optical.
options.prompt: Add subtle radial chromatic aberration: render red and blue channel copies (feColorMatrix channel isolation) scaled 1.004 and 0.996 around the frame center and composite with screen, so fringes are 0 at center and 2-3px at the corners. Spike to 6-8px for 3-4 frames on punch-ins, then ease back. Never exceed 2px on text at rest.

options.what: A deliberate digital offset of the red, green and blue channels by a uniform amount in a chosen direction.
options.looks: Visible red and cyan (or RGB) ghost copies of shapes and type offset sideways; graphic and glitchy rather than optical.
options.motion: Offsets jump on beats and transitions, often stepped, then snap back to aligned.
options.use: Glitch, cyber and gaming aesthetics, music visuals, social content, impact accents on type.
options.vs: Chromatic aberration is radial and optical; RGB split is uniform and digital. Glitch combines RGB split with slicing and noise.
options.prompt: On impact beats, split the element into red and cyan copies (feColorMatrix or tinted duplicates with mix-blend-mode: screen on dark, multiply on light) offset 4-10px horizontally in opposite directions for 2-4 frames, stepped, then snap back to aligned. Use on at most one element per beat; never leave a split on readable text for more than 4 frames.

options.what: Brief bursts of simulated digital corruption: displaced slices, channel splits, blocks and noise.
options.looks: For a few frames the image tears into horizontal slices shifted sideways, colors separate, blocks of wrong color appear; then it is clean again.
options.motion: Irregular stepped bursts of 2-8 frames, usually on beats, transitions or 'error' moments.
options.use: Tech and security themes, AI and cyber aesthetics, gaming, music, error or hack story beats.
options.vs: Glitch texture is persistent; glitch as an effect is a burst. Glitch transition cuts between scenes with it. VHS is analog damage.
options.prompt: Trigger glitch bursts only at story beats: for 3-6 frames, slice the element or frame into 4-8 horizontal bands (clip-path inset copies), offset each band 8-60px on x on a stepped schedule, add a 4px RGB split and one or two flat color blocks, then snap back clean. Use fixed offsets per frame (no unseeded randomness) so renders are deterministic.

options.what: Pixels shifted according to a map (noise, gradient, image or texture) so shapes warp, ripple or melt.
options.looks: Wavy, rippled, heat-haze or liquid warping of type, images and shapes; the warp follows the pattern of the map.
options.motion: The map scrolls or evolves over time, making surfaces flow; displacement amount ramps up and down for transitions.
options.use: Liquid and organic transitions, heat or water effects, experimental type, refraction fakes.
options.vs: Distortion is the broader family of warps (bulge, twirl, stretch); displacement specifically uses a map. Refraction is displacement used to mimic glass.
options.prompt: Warp the element with an SVG feDisplacementMap fed by feTurbulence (fractalNoise, baseFrequency 0.01-0.03, numOctaves 2). Animate the warp by tweening the displacement scale (0 at rest, 30-80 at peak) and the turbulence baseFrequency slowly on the timeline. For transitions, ramp scale up while the old scene fades and back to 0 as the new one resolves (500-800ms total).

options.what: Geometric warping of shapes or images: bulge, pinch, twirl, stretch, wave or perspective skew.
options.looks: Type and images bent, bulged, twisted or rippled in controlled ways; can be playful (bulge) or unsettling (twirl).
options.motion: Warps ramp in and out on emphasis or transitions; a wave travels through type; a bulge follows the cursor.
options.use: Experimental and kinetic typography, music and fashion motion, playful emphasis, transitions.
options.conveys: Play, experimentation, instability or surrealism depending on degree.
options.vs: Displacement is map-driven warping, one kind of distortion. Lens distortion and fisheye are optical distortions. Stretch and squash (motion language) deform the object's transform, not its pixels.
options.prompt: Distort with intent and a single type per piece: wave (SVG text on a path, or per-letter y offsets following a sine with 8-16px amplitude traveling across over 1s), bulge (radial displacement map, scale 30-60, centered on the focus), or stretch (scaleY 1.3 to 1 on selected letters). Ramp distortion in over 200ms and out over 300ms; nothing stays distorted during a read.

options.what: A film-grain pass applied on top of the finished composite to unify it and remove digital sterility.
options.looks: Fine organic speckle over everything, strongest in midtones; gradients stop banding; graphics feel filmed.
options.motion: Re-rolls every frame (or at 12 fps for a softer, stop-motion feel).
options.use: Cinematic brand films, gradient-heavy SaaS heroes, editorial and documentary pieces.
options.vs: Film grain in texture is the same look chosen as surface; use this when grain is a finishing pass over otherwise clean design. Noise is harsher and digital.
options.prompt: Finish the composite with a full-frame grain pass: feTurbulence fractalNoise (baseFrequency 0.85, numOctaves 3), desaturated, mix-blend-mode: overlay at 6-10%, above everything. Re-roll per frame by tweening the seed attribute with ease steps(frames). Do not vary grain strength between scenes.

options.what: Harsh, chromatic, pixel-level random noise applied as an effect, from subtle dither to TV static.
options.looks: Crisp colored speckle; at high intensity, full-frame static snow.
options.motion: Re-rolls every frame; surges briefly on transitions, signal loss or glitch beats.
options.use: Tech and cyber themes, transition accents, signal and broadcast metaphors.
options.vs: Grain is organic and luminance-based; noise is crisp, chromatic and digital. Digital noise in texture is the persistent version.
options.prompt: Use noise as an accent: feTurbulence type turbulence (baseFrequency 2, numOctaves 1), color channels kept, screen blend. At rest 0-4% opacity; on signal-loss or transition beats surge to 50-80% for 4-8 frames, re-rolling every frame with a stepped seed tween, then cut back.

options.what: Horizontal line pattern of a CRT or interlaced display laid over the image.
options.looks: Fine dark horizontal lines across everything; often with slight glow and vignette.
options.motion: Static lines with a slow rolling brighter band, or flicker on transitions.
options.use: Retro-computing and terminal aesthetics, sci-fi HUDs, gaming, surveillance themes.
options.vs: CRT scanlines in texture is the persistent look; here it is an effect pass that may be applied to a single element (a screen within the scene). VHS is tape damage, not display lines.
options.prompt: Overlay scanlines on the target element or frame: repeating-linear-gradient(to bottom, rgba(0,0,0,0.22) 0 1px, transparent 1px 3px), plus a soft brighter band (8% of height, 4% white) rolling down every 6s. For a screen within the scene, clip scanlines to that screen only.

options.what: Analog videotape artifacts applied as an effect: chroma bleed, tracking bars, jitter and soft resolution.
options.looks: Soft image, color smearing sideways, noise bands, tracking distortion near the bottom, washed blacks.
options.motion: Constant micro-jitter with occasional tracking glitches and rewind-style warps.
options.use: Nostalgic transitions, found-footage beats, retro music and brand pieces.
options.vs: VHS texture is persistent; the effect version is used for a segment or transition (e.g. a 'rewind' moment). Glitch is digital; VHS is analog.
options.prompt: Apply a VHS effect to a segment: soft blur 0.6px, red/blue chroma bleed offsets of plus or minus 2-3px (screen blend), lifted blacks, a 30px noisy tracking band near the bottom, and 1-2px horizontal jitter stepped every 2 frames. For a rewind beat, add a 400ms burst of horizontal skew bands and reversed motion.

options.what: Fading after-images left behind a moving object, as if the frame retains its recent positions.
options.looks: A comet-like tail of progressively fainter copies or a continuous streak behind a moving element.
options.motion: Trails lengthen with speed and fade out 150-500ms after the object stops.
options.use: Kinetic type, cursor and gesture emphasis, energetic transitions, music visuals.
options.conveys: Speed, flow, energy, time made visible.
options.vs: Echo is discrete, evenly spaced repeats that can persist as a pattern; trails decay continuously. Motion blur blurs the object; trails leave separate after-images.
options.prompt: Create trails with 5-8 clones of the moving element that follow the same tween with increasing delays (20-30ms each) and decreasing opacity (60% down to 5%), optionally with growing blur. Clones fade to 0 within 300ms after the move ends. Trails only on fast moves; never on text that must be read mid-move.

options.what: Discrete repeated copies of an element offset in time or space, forming a rhythmic pattern.
options.looks: Stacked or fanned duplicates of type or shapes at regular intervals, often alternating colors or outlines; op-art and Swiss poster quality.
options.motion: Copies follow the leader with fixed time offsets, creating cascades, spirals and ripples that can hold as a composition.
options.use: Kinetic typography, title sequences, brand motion systems, music visuals, logo animation.
options.conveys: Rhythm, repetition, hypnotic energy, graphic confidence.
options.vs: Trails are decaying after-images of movement; echo is a designed repetition that can hold still. Named after the After Effects Echo effect and repeater tools.
options.prompt: Echo the element as 6-12 copies with a fixed time offset (60-100ms each) along the same tween, alternating fill and outline (or two palette colors), each copy offset in scale or position by a constant step. The final state can hold as a static pattern for 1-2s before copies collapse back into one.

options.what: A classical animation device: for one or two frames the object is stretched or multiplied along its path to bridge a very fast move.
options.looks: On the fast frame, a shape becomes an elongated streak or a row of partial copies, then snaps back to its normal form.
options.motion: Lasts 1-3 frames at the peak of a snap move; invisible at normal playback except as a sense of speed and cartoon energy.
options.use: Cartoon and character animation, playful UI and icon motion, snappy kinetic type.
options.conveys: Cartoon energy, snappiness, handmade animation craft.
options.vs: Motion blur is optical and soft; a smear is a drawn deformation with hard edges. Stretch (motion language) is a sustained deformation; a smear lasts one or two frames.
options.prompt: On the fastest snap moves, insert a 1-2 frame smear: set scaleX to 2-3x along the direction of travel (transform-origin at the trailing edge) with the element halfway to its target, then snap to normal scale at the destination. Use hard edges (no blur). Only on moves that cover more than 30% of the frame in under 150ms.

options.what: Many small elements (dots, sparks, confetti, shapes) emitted and moved as a system.
options.looks: Bursts of confetti or sparks, drifting fields of dots, flows of points forming shapes; density and size vary.
options.motion: Emit, travel under velocity, gravity and drag, then fade; or flow along paths and assemble into logos or type.
options.use: Celebrations and success states, logo assemblies, AI and data themes, ambient backgrounds.
options.conveys: Celebration, energy, abundance, magic or data depending on shape.
options.vs: Dust is a sparse, slow atmospheric particle layer; particles are an active system. Fragmentation breaks an existing object; particles are emitted.
options.prompt: Build particle systems on a canvas (or 30-150 absolutely positioned DOM nodes for small counts) with a seeded pseudo-random generator; compute each particle's position as a pure function of timeline time (p = origin + v*t + 0.5*g*t^2, with drag) so the system is seek-safe. Bursts: 40-120 particles, lifetime 600-1200ms, fading and shrinking over the last 40%. Use palette colors only.

options.what: Sparse, slow atmospheric particles floating in the scene, catching light.
options.looks: A few soft points drifting at different depths, some blurred, some sharp, catching light in beams.
options.motion: Very slow drift (5-20px per second) with gentle turbulence; parallax between near and far motes.
options.use: Cinematic environments, product hero shots, calm brand films, luxury and ambient loops.
options.vs: Dust as texture is specks on the film surface; dust as effect is motes floating in the scene with depth. Particles are an active emitted system.
options.prompt: Scatter 20-60 motes across 3 depth bands: near (4-8px, blurred 3px, 30% opacity), mid (2-3px, sharp, 50%), far (1px, 30%). Drift each on a seeded slow path (5-20px per second, sine-based wobble as a function of timeline time), with near motes moving fastest. Brighten motes inside any light beam.

options.what: Soft, turbulent volumes of smoke, fog or vapor that billow, curl and dissipate.
options.looks: Wispy gray or colored volumes with soft edges and swirling internal detail; fog layers softening depth.
options.motion: Slow billowing and curling, rising and dissipating; reveals as smoke clears.
options.use: Dramatic reveals, cinematic titles, product launches (smoke-clearing reveal), mystery and atmosphere.
options.vs: Displacement can warp an image like heat haze but has no volume; smoke is a visible medium. True volumetric smoke needs simulation.
options.prompt: Approximate smoke with 3-5 large layers of feTurbulence fractal noise (baseFrequency 0.005-0.012, numOctaves 4) used as alpha masks on a smoke-colored fill, each layer drifting and slowly changing baseFrequency at a different speed, with soft radial masks for edges. For a reveal, fade layers out outward from the center over 1.5-2.5s. Photoreal volumetric smoke requires pre-rendered footage or a WebGL shader.

options.what: Physically simulated fluid: pours, splashes, drips and waves that obey fluid dynamics.
options.looks: Realistic splashes and pours with droplets, crowns and surface tension; or stylized gooey fluid that still behaves physically.
options.motion: Momentum, gravity, viscosity and surface tension drive every movement; nothing is keyframed by hand.
options.use: Beverage, cosmetics and food films, abstract 3D brand motion, satisfying product reveals.
options.vs: Liquid (material) and gooey 2D blobs can be keyframed; liquid simulation computes the motion. Liquid transitions borrow the look without physics.
options.prompt: Treat true liquid simulation as out of scope for a live HTML build: use pre-rendered simulation footage (alpha-channel video) composited as a clip, or a WebGL fluid shader driven deterministically by timeline time. For stylized 2D fluid, use gooey metaball blobs (blur plus alpha-threshold SVG filter) keyframed to mimic gravity and viscosity: accelerate downward with power2.in, stretch drips before they separate.

options.what: Physically simulated fabric that drapes, folds, flutters and collides with objects.
options.looks: Sheets and banners with realistic folds, cloth reveals sliding off products, fabric flags rippling.
options.motion: Gravity, wind and collision drive the fabric; follow-through and settling happen naturally.
options.use: Product unveilings (cloth pull reveal), fashion and textile brands, abstract 3D brand films.
options.vs: Fabric (material) is the substance; cloth simulation is the physics-driven motion of it. A flag wave via displacement is a cheap 2D approximation.
options.prompt: Treat true cloth simulation as pre-rendered footage (alpha-channel video) or a WebGL verlet cloth stepped deterministically from timeline time. For a 2D approximation, animate a mesh-like SVG path or clip-path whose control points follow a delayed, overshooting sequence (each row lagging 30-50ms behind the one above) with an feDisplacementMap ripple on top, sliding off the object in 900-1400ms.

options.what: Objects that deform, wobble and recover under force according to simulated elasticity.
options.looks: Squishy objects that dent on contact, jiggle and ripple, pile up and squash against each other.
options.motion: Impacts propagate through the body, oscillate with damping and settle; colliding bodies deform each other.
options.use: Playful product and brand motion, satisfying loops, soft 3D and clay styles, toy-like UI.
options.vs: Squash and stretch (motion language) is hand-keyed deformation; soft-body simulation computes it. Jelly (material) describes the substance; this is the physics.
options.prompt: Approximate soft bodies in 2D with keyed damped oscillation: on impact, scaleY 0.8/scaleX 1.2 then oscillate (1.1/0.92, 0.96/1.04, 1/1) over 600-900ms with elastic.out(1, 0.35), transform-origin at the contact point; for blobs, move SVG path control points with staggered springs (30-60ms lag). Real multi-body soft-body collision requires WebGL physics or pre-rendered footage.

options.what: An object breaks into sharp shards that fly apart, as glass or a brittle solid shattering.
options.looks: Angular shards (Voronoi or radial cracks) bursting outward with rotation, catching light, falling under gravity.
options.motion: A crack propagates from an impact point, then shards explode outward fast (100-200ms), rotate and decelerate or fall.
options.use: Dramatic reveals, 'breaking through' metaphors (barriers, limits), sports, gaming and action titles.
options.vs: Fragmentation breaks into pieces in an orderly or graphic way (tiles, strips) and can reassemble; shattering is violent and irregular. Particles are emitted, not broken from an object.
options.prompt: Shatter by pre-cutting the element into 12-30 Voronoi or radial polygons (clip-path copies, fixed seed) around the impact point. Flash cracks for 2-3 frames, then fly shards outward: velocity inversely proportional to distance from impact, rotation 90-360 degrees, expo.out over 400-600ms, followed by gravity drift and fade. Reveal the next scene behind the shards.

options.what: An object splits into many regular or graphic pieces (tiles, strips, dots) that scatter, drift or reassemble.
options.looks: An image or shape breaking into a grid of tiles, slices or dots that separate with order and rhythm, then reform into something else.
options.motion: Staggered separation (by row, radius or noise), drift, and reassembly into the next form; reversible and controlled.
options.use: Transitions, data and AI metaphors (information breaking down and rebuilding), logo builds, tech launch films.
options.conveys: Transformation, systems, digital construction and deconstruction.
options.vs: Shattering is violent and irregular; fragmentation is orderly and often reversible. Pixel dissolve (transition) is a flat fade pattern, not pieces moving.
options.prompt: Fragment the element into a regular grid (8x8 to 16x16 tiles, each a clipped copy or a canvas tile). Scatter tiles with a stagger based on distance from a focal point (15-25ms per ring), translating 50-300px and rotating up to 45 degrees over 500-700ms with power3.inOut, then reassemble them into the next form with the reverse stagger. Keep the grid visible in the motion.
